‘Unless you mean to call Miss Havisham a man. And I doubt even you would go that far.’

‘Miss Havisham, up in town?’ said Joe.

‘Is there a Miss Havisham down in town?’ my sister replied.

‘She wants this boy to go and play at her house. And naturally he's going. And he'd better play when he gets there,’ said my sister, shaking her head at me to encourage an extremely cheerful and playful mood, ‘or I'll make him work.’

I had heard of Miss Havisham up in town—everyone for miles around had heard of her. She was said to be an enormously rich, grim woman who lived alone in a large, gloomy house barricaded against burglars.

‘Well, I never!’ said Joe, astonished. ‘I wonder how she got to know Pip!’

‘Idiot!’ my sister cried. ‘Who said she knew him?’

‘Someone,’ Joe politely suggested again, ‘did mention that she wanted him to go and play there.’

‘And couldn't she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew a boy who could come and play there? Isn't it just possible that Uncle Pumblechook rents property from her, and that he sometimes—we won't say every three months or six months, since that would be asking too much of you—but sometimes visits her to pay his rent? And couldn't she ask him then whether he knew a boy who could come and play? And couldn't Uncle Pumblechook, who is always so thoughtful and considerate toward us—though you may not appreciate it, Joseph,’ she said with the deepest reproach, as though he were the most heartless nephew alive, ‘then mention this boy, standing here prancing about’—which I solemnly declare I was not—‘for whom I've always been a willing slave?’

‘Excellent again!’ cried Uncle Pumblechook. ‘Well said! Nicely put! Excellent indeed! Now, Joseph, you understand the situation.’

‘No, Joseph,’ said my sister, still reproaching him, while Joe repeatedly rubbed the back of his hand across his nose in apology, ‘you do not understand it yet, whatever you may think. You may suppose you do, but you do not, Joseph. Because you don't know that Uncle Pumblechook realizes this visit to Miss Havisham might, for all we know, make the boy's fortune. He has offered to take him into town tonight in his own carriage, put him up for the night, and personally take him to Miss Havisham's tomorrow morning. And goodness help me!’ my sister cried, throwing off her bonnet in sudden desperation. ‘Here I am talking to a pair of fools, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the mare catching cold outside, and the boy covered in soot and dirt from head to foot!’

For years, Dorian Gray remained under the influence of this book. Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that he never tried to escape it. He ordered no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition from Paris and had each bound in a different colour, to match his shifting moods and the changing whims of a temperament that sometimes seemed almost entirely beyond his control. The hero, that remarkable young Parisian whose nature so strangely combined romanticism with a scientific disposition, became for him a kind of advance portrait of himself. Indeed, the entire book seemed to tell the story of his own life before he had lived it.

In one respect he was more fortunate than the novel's extraordinary hero. He never experienced—never, indeed, had any reason to experience—that rather grotesque fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water which overtook the young Parisian so early in life, brought on by the sudden decline of what had apparently once been remarkable beauty. With an almost cruel delight—and perhaps cruelty has a place in nearly every joy, as it certainly does in every pleasure—he would read the book's later sections. They gave a truly tragic, if somewhat overstated, account of the grief and despair of someone who had himself lost the thing he valued most in other people and in the world.

For the extraordinary beauty that had so captivated Basil Hallward, and many others besides, seemed never to desert him. Even people who had heard the worst stories about him—and from time to time strange rumours of his way of life spread through London and became the talk of the clubs—could believe nothing disgraceful of him once they saw him. He always looked like someone who had kept himself untouched by the world's corruption. Men exchanging coarse remarks fell silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. The purity of his face seemed to rebuke them. His presence alone appeared to bring back memories of the innocence they had spoiled. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have escaped the stains of an age that was both sordid and sensual.

Often, after returning home from one of the mysterious, lengthy absences that inspired such strange speculation among his friends, or those who believed themselves his friends, he would steal upstairs to the locked room. He would unlock the door with the key he now always carried, then stand holding a mirror before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted. His eyes would move from the wicked, ageing face on the canvas to the beautiful young face laughing back at him from the polished glass.

‘I then reasoned backward from the facts. The murderers had escaped through one of these windows. If that was true, they could not have fastened the windows again from inside, as we found them. This obvious difficulty had stopped the police from investigating further in that direction. Yet the windows were fastened. They must therefore be able to fasten themselves. There was no avoiding that conclusion. I went to the window that was not blocked, pulled out its nail with some difficulty, and tried to lift the sliding frame. It would not move, however hard I tried, just as I had expected. Now I knew there must be a hidden spring. This confirmation persuaded me that at least my starting assumptions were right, although the nails remained a mystery. A careful search soon revealed the spring. I pressed it and, satisfied with my discovery, left the window closed.

‘I then put the nail back and studied it closely. Someone climbing out through this window could have closed it behind them, allowing the spring to catch. But they could not have replaced the nail. The conclusion was clear, and once again it narrowed my search. The murderers must have escaped through the other window. If both frames had the same springs, as seemed likely, then there must be a difference between the nails, or at least in how they were fitted. I climbed onto the bed's canvas support and examined the second window closely over the headboard. Reaching down behind the board, I easily found and pressed the spring. As I had expected, it was just like the other one. Next I examined the nail. It was equally thick and seemed to be fitted in exactly the same way, driven in almost to its head.

‘You may say I must have been puzzled. If so, you have misunderstood my reasoning. To borrow a term from hunting, I had never once lost the trail. Not for an instant had the scent disappeared. Every link in the chain of reasoning was sound. I had followed the secret to its final point, and that point was the nail. As I have said, it looked in every way like the nail in the other window. But that fact, convincing though it might seem, counted for nothing beside the knowledge that the trail ended here, at this very spot. “There must be something wrong with the nail,” I said. I touched it, and the head, with about a quarter of an inch of the shaft, came away in my fingers.’
